title: Why the highlands are white
teaches: White crystals in Apollo 11's soil, the ocean of magma that floated the Moon's crust, and where the mare lavas came from

parts.title: White grains in a dark sea

blocks.text: Apollo 11 landed on the Sea of Tranquility, a mare plain, and its rocks were what everyone expected: dark basalt, the kind of lava rock studied in lesson 4, crystallised from a melt and full of dark minerals. Mixed into the soil, though, were small grains that did not fit. A few per cent of the fragments were white, and they were made almost entirely of one mineral, **plagioclase feldspar**, a pale mineral built, like most rock-forming minerals, from silicon and oxygen (a silicate), with calcium, aluminium and sodium. Feldspars are the most common minerals in Earth's crust, but rocks made of plagioclase alone are rare.

In the months after the samples reached laboratories in late 1969, John Wood's group at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory in Cambridge, Massachusetts, sorted more than 1,600 rock fragments from the soil. Wood argued that the white ones could not come from the mare. They had been thrown in by impacts from the bright highlands tens of kilometres away, and since the highlands are bright everywhere, he proposed that the highland crust itself was made of this nearly pure plagioclase rock, called **anorthosite**. Apollo 16, which landed in the highlands in 1972, brought back rock that bore him out. That explained why the highlands are bright: plagioclase is white, and basalt, full of dark iron-rich minerals, is not.

blocks.caption: Anorthosite, a rock made almost entirely of plagioclase feldspar.

blocks.text: The proposal raised a harder question. On Earth, anorthosite occurs in scattered bodies a few kilometres to tens of kilometres across. The Moon's highlands cover more than four-fifths of its surface, and the crust beneath them averages 30 to 50 kilometres thick, measured later from the timing of moonquake waves at seismometers the crews left behind (as in lesson D3's method for the Earth) and from small changes in the pull of the Moon's gravity on orbiting spacecraft. How does a whole world acquire a crust made of one mineral?

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Apollo 11's mare soil held white fragments made almost entirely of plagioclase feldspar.
John Wood argued they came from the highlands, so the highland crust is anorthosite, which is why it is bright.
A crust tens of kilometres thick made of one mineral needed an explanation.

blocks.text: Lesson 4 showed what happens as a melt cools: crystals of different minerals form one after another, as the temperature falls past each one's freezing point. In a thin lava flow they freeze where they grow. In a large, slowly cooling body of melt they have time to move, and they move according to their density. A crystal denser than the liquid around it sinks; one lighter than the liquid floats. Geologists see this in layered intrusions on Earth, where dense crystals of olivine (a green iron and magnesium silicate) have settled into beds at the bottom of a cooled magma chamber like sand settling in water (lesson 2).

Wood's group, and independently Joseph Smith's group at the University of Chicago, proposed at the first Lunar Science Conference in January 1970 that the outer part of the young Moon had been entirely molten: a **magma ocean** perhaps several hundred kilometres deep. As it cooled, the first crystals to form were olivine and then pyroxene, both dense, iron- and magnesium-rich minerals. They sank and piled up as the Moon's mantle. Only after most of the ocean had crystallised did plagioclase begin to form, and plagioclase, at about 2.7 grams per cubic centimetre, is lighter than the iron-rich liquid that remained, at about 2.9. It rose and gathered at the top as a floating crust of anorthosite.

blocks.caption: A column through the Moon's magma ocean, from the surface to its floor. Minerals form in the order and amounts estimated for the lunar ocean, simplified; each crystal sinks or floats by its density against the melt's.
blocks.task: Cool the ocean until a white crust forms at the real melt density

blocks.text: The young Earth probably had magma oceans too, yet it does not have a crust like this. Its melts were wetter and under higher pressure down deep, so they crystallised differently, and whatever crust they made has since been recycled by plate tectonics many times over. The Moon is dry and has no plates, so its first crust, more than 4.3 billion years old, survives, battered by impacts but still in place.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Crystals forming in a large body of melt sink or float according to their density compared with the liquid.
In the lunar magma ocean, dense olivine and pyroxene sank to form the mantle; light plagioclase floated to form the anorthosite crust.
The Moon's dryness and lack of plate tectonics let that first crust survive.

blocks.text: The crew of Apollo 15 knew the idea before they launched. Their geology teacher, the Caltech geologist Leon Silver, had trained them to look for pale, coarse-grained highland rock. On 1 August 1971, on the lower slope of the Apennine Mountains at the rim of a small crater called Spur, Dave Scott and Jim Irwin saw a white fragment perched on a dusty clod of soil. Scott radioed: "Guess what we just found! I think we found what we came for."

blocks.caption: Apollo 15 at the edge of Hadley Rille, a winding channel cut by flowing lava, with the Apennine Mountains behind.

blocks.text: The rock, numbered 15415 and nicknamed the Genesis Rock by the press, is almost pure plagioclase. It turned out to be about 4 billion years old. Its crystals show damage from shock and heat, and its radioactive clock was reset or disturbed by later events, so 4 billion years dates that history rather than the crust's first formation. Other anorthosites, from Apollo 16 in the highlands and from Apollo 15, give ages up to about 4.36 billion years, close to the time the magma ocean finished crystallising.

blocks.caption: The Genesis Rock, sample 15415, about 9 cm across. It is almost entirely plagioclase feldspar.

blocks.text: The magma ocean predicted something else. As crystals were removed, the elements whose atoms fit poorly into any of them[^incompatible] were left behind and concentrated in the last few per cent of liquid, trapped between the floating crust and the sunken mantle. Apollo samples contain just such a material, strangely rich in potassium (chemical symbol K), the rare earth elements (REE, a family of fifteen similar metals) and phosphorus (P), and named **KREEP** from those initials. It is also rich in uranium and thorium, and so, with its potassium, mildly radioactive. The mare basalts carry a second clue. They are short of europium, the one rare earth element that plagioclase builds into its crystals readily, because much of the Moon's europium had already been carried off into the floating crust before their source rock melted.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Apollo 15 found the Genesis Rock, a piece of anorthosite crust about 4 billion years old.
Highland anorthosites date to as old as about 4.36 billion years.
KREEP, rich in potassium, rare earth elements and phosphorus, is the residue of the magma ocean's last liquid.

parts.title: Where the dark lava came from

blocks.text: If the crust is white anorthosite, the dark maria are something added later. Most Apollo mare basalts are 3.1 to 3.9 billion years old (lesson P2), hundreds of millions of years younger than the crust. They formed when parts of the mantle, the pile of sunken olivine and pyroxene, warmed by radioactive elements, partly melted. The melt rose and erupted where the crust was thinnest: in the floors of the giant impact basins, hundreds of kilometres across, dug out during the heavy early bombardment.

That is why most maria are round in outline. Nearly all of them lie on the side of the Moon facing Earth, where gravity mapping from orbit (most precisely by NASA's GRAIL spacecraft in 2012)[^grail] shows the crust is thinner, and where much of the KREEP and its radioactive heat is concentrated. The Soviet probe Luna 3 photographed the far side in 1959,[^farside] and it surprised everyone: there are almost no maria there at all. Mare lavas cover about 17 per cent of the Moon's surface but make up only about 1 per cent of its crust; they are a thin dark coating, a few hundred metres to a few kilometres thick, poured into basins in a white world.

blocks.caption: The full Moon, with the dark maria filling round basins on the side that faces Earth.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The maria are basalt from partial melting of the Moon's mantle, erupted mostly 3.1 to 3.9 billion years ago.
The lava filled giant impact basins, mostly on the near side, where the crust is thinner.
The maria are a thin coating, about a sixth of the surface but around 1 per cent of the crust.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the Moon's crust
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why are the Moon's highlands bright and the maria dark?
choices: The highlands are anorthosite, made of white plagioclase; the maria are basalt, rich in dark iron-bearing minerals
The highlands are covered in ice; the maria are bare rock
The highlands catch more sunlight because they are higher
items.why: Rock colour follows its minerals. Plagioclase is white; basalt is full of dark pyroxene and iron-titanium oxides.

items.ask: In a cooling magma ocean, what decides whether a crystal ends up at the top or the bottom?
choices: Whether it is denser or less dense than the liquid around it
items.why: Like a stone or a cork in water, a crystal sinks if it is denser than the melt and floats if it is lighter.

items.ask: Why did plagioclase float in the lunar magma ocean?
choices: It is lighter than the iron-rich melt that remained when it began to form
It formed first, before the melt had time to cool
Gas bubbles carried it to the surface
items.why: Plagioclase, at about 2.7 g/cm³, is less dense than the iron-rich liquid, about 2.9 g/cm³, left after olivine and pyroxene had crystallised and sunk.

choices: The last liquid of the magma ocean, rich in elements that did not fit into the main minerals
The oldest part of the anorthosite crust
Glass beads from lunar fire fountains
items.why: Potassium (K), rare earth elements and phosphorus stayed in the melt as crystals formed, and ended up concentrated in its last few per cent.

items.ask: Why are the maria mostly on the side of the Moon facing Earth?
choices: The crust is thinner on that side, so mantle melts could reach the surface in the basins there
Earth's gravity pulled lava toward it
Fewer impacts struck the far side
items.why: Mare basalt rose from the mantle and erupted where the crust was thinnest: in the floors of near-side impact basins.

items.ask: What is this rock, and what did it support?
choices: The Genesis Rock, a piece of anorthosite crust supporting the magma ocean idea
A mare basalt from Apollo 11, showing the Moon is volcanic
A meteorite that formed a lunar crater
items.why: Sample 15415, collected on Apollo 15, is almost pure plagioclase, the kind of rock a floating magma-ocean crust should be made of.

summary: **The bright highlands are anorthosite.** Almost pure plagioclase feldspar, which is why they are white.
**The young Moon had a magma ocean.** As it crystallised, dense minerals sank to form the mantle and light plagioclase floated up as the crust.
**The last liquid was KREEP.** It concentrated the elements that did not fit into the crystals.
**The crust is very old.** Anorthosites date back to about 4.36 billion years.
**The dark maria came later.** Basalt lavas filled giant impact basins, mostly on the near side.

grail.title: Twin spacecraft
grail.text: GRAIL was two spacecraft, Ebb and Flow, flying one behind the other. Each time the leader passed over denser rock, its extra pull sped it up and the gap between them changed by a few micrometres, which the pair measured with radio signals. At the end of the mission both were flown into a mountain near the north pole.

farside.title: The far side
farside.text: The far side is not dark: it gets as much sunlight as the near side, at the opposite phase. It is only hidden, because the Moon turns once on its axis for each orbit, keeping one face toward the Earth.

incompatible.title: Incompatible elements
incompatible.text: Geologists call an element incompatible when its atoms are the wrong size or carry the wrong electrical charge to fit neatly into the crystal lattices of common mantle minerals like olivine and pyroxene. When rock melts, these elements prefer the liquid; when melt crystallises, they stay behind until the very end.
